thread.title: Microsoft 3.0: A Turnaround That Looks Real

author: admin
title: Microsoft 3.0: A Turnaround That Looks Real
text:

This widespread growth suggests widespread management competence, not just at the CEO level but below it. That’s a refreshing thing to say about Microsoft.
A note about Microsoft, AWS and the Cloud
There is no one defined way to think about success in “the Cloud.”
Amazon defines its AWS (Amazon Web Services) one way, with $5.4 billion in revenue in the March quarter. Microsoft defined “Intelligent Cloud” above as having $2.7 billion revenues, and by that comparison, it is half the size of AWS. However, also in the 10-K (p. 37), Microsoft redefines the segment this way:
Our commercial cloud revenue, which primarily comprises Office 365 commercial, Azure, Dynamics 365, and other cloud properties, was $6.0 billion and $16.3 billion for the three and nine months ended March 31, 2018, respectively, and $3.8 billion and $10.4 billion for the three and nine months ended March 31, 2017, respectively.
By the above definition, Microsoft’s Cloud is larger than that of Amazon, and given all the software services there that should have very high margins, I will bet it is, or will prove to be, inherently more profitable.
Given Microsoft’s many business relationships, I expect it to do very well in the Cloud, no matter how it is defined. Heavy capital spending and other growth-related costs mean that current profits likely understate the ultimate profitability of Microsoft as a Cloud-centric company, thus helping shareholders to look past the current P/E.
R&D and other capital allocation looking solid
The sales growth is occurring, while R&D is growing almost as fast as sales, comprising 13% of revenues in Q3. R&D is pushing enhancements in the Cloud, to Cortana, to AI in general, to the “mixed reality” HoloLens devices, to Xbox and the resuscitation of Kinect, the expected improvements to Windows and especially Office as a service, etc.
When a company of Microsoft’s size, dominance and overall economies of scale spends 13% of revenues on R&D and shows sales growth in all its segments, investors have a further reason not to focus unduly on P/E.
The company looks to be allocating its free cash flows well, including spending heavily on plant and equipment for its Cloud businesses globally.
Microsoft has been increasing spending on the productive parts of the business, namely R&D and sales and marketing, while holding G&A stable (see p. 3 of the 10-Q). That’s a positive sign for management’s effectiveness and seriousness about growing.
Moving on, what impresses me the most about the company is that it finally may have done a big deal that looks good and could end up great.
LinkedIn may be the turnaround “tell”
One aspect of the LinkedIn, or LI, deal that looks good is the rapid growth in revenues, from $976 million in Q3 2017 to $1.335 billion last quarter; note that amortization charges make the GAAP numbers still show a loss from LI. The 37% yoy increase is more than double the 15.6% increase for all of Microsoft’s revenues. From Satya Nadella’s prepared remarks in the conference call (emphasis added):
From the start, we recognized the opportunity for LinkedIn and Microsoft to combine forces to create economic opportunity for every member of the global workforce and enable professionals to be more productive and successful. A little over one year in, we feel great about the value we are delivering for members, customers and shareholders.
Our integration model has enabled LinkedIn to accelerate growth, while retaining its member-first ethos. Results are ahead of expectations across all lines of business with revenue growth of 37% year-over-year. We saw record levels of engagement again this quarter with sessions growth of more than 30% year-over-year, driven by innovation across the platform. This increased engagement is driving strong demand for sponsored content and marketing solutions and record levels of job postings and job visitors again this quarter in Talent Solutions.
All lines of LI’s business beat expectations. This homogeneity of good news is a sort of fractal to the bigger story that Microsoft grew broadly across all its business lines.
A second positive about the LI deal is discussed in, for example, a Wired article from March 2017, “Now We Know Why Microsoft Bought LinkedIn.” This emphasizes that LI founder Reid Hoffman joined Microsoft’s board as part of the acquisition. With the chairman of the board, John Thompson, also a Silicon Valley insider, it is felt that Microsoft may make more personnel and deal progress. As the Wired article puts it:
Among a core group of constituents for whom Microsoft may not factor into conversation, Hoffman will work to raise its profile. The trickle-down effect has the potential to be tremendous as Microsoft competes for partners and talent.
Just as one bad Ballmer deal led to another, if LI indeed is as good for Microsoft as it could be, this may be only the beginning.
A few more points on LI:
How big can LinkedIn get? Perhaps very big
As LI moves first toward GAAP profitability, and then to its first billion members, it could be another category-killing monster reminiscent of Facebook (NASDAQ:FB). FB’s growth could well be a template for that of LI. In the 4 years from 2013 to 2017, FB grew revenues about 50% each year, from $7.9 billion in 2013 to $40.7 billion in 2017. Net income before extraordinary items rose much faster, from $1.5 billion in 2013 to $18.2 billion in 2017.
By analogy, LI has major profit potential in its own right for Microsoft.
In addition, as a B2B site, not (for now) a direct competitor to FB, it can provide additive and perhaps even synergistic benefits with Microsoft’s Cloud offerings.
With some patience as the site’s functionality and member base continue to be built out and integrated within Microsoft, there could be large and rapidly growing profits from LI. This possibility may not be incorporated in Microsoft’s valuation.
Another positive, really lack of a negative, is that:
Insider selling has been very limited
E-Trade’s data shows that except for some relatively modest sales by a senior executive, Christopher Capossela, there have been very few sales by insiders for the past year. That’s quite a rarity in the tech sector given the run that Microsoft has experienced.
Limited insider selling suggests that the company is on track. The lack of insider accumulation is normal for tech stocks in bull trends.
Some thoughts on the transitional period
As Microsoft moves to a Cloud-centric and AI-centric B2B model, and also becomes more integrated in some ways – even designing chips – there are many significant upside possibilities and downside risks. These are too numerous to discuss in one article; a relevant and accessible one is discussed in an analysis in The Verge. This involves the decision to split Windows development into two teams. The article’s author muses in his conclusion:
But as the teams responsible for Windows drift apart from each other, communication will likely become more formal. Ultimately, the platform and experiences teams have fundamentally different customers, and therefore will have fundamentally different priorities. This could create friction, duplicate effort, and, if not carefully managed, a platform that doesnt truly serve the experiences of Microsofts consumer customers.
I already feel this a bit… Am I a customer Microsoft even wants to keep?
… Microsofts increased focus on serving businesses and ceding ground on consumer products sounds a lot like IBM.
Ceding ground on consumer products = ceding ground on PCs. Because the Nadella era has led to upside surprises in both sales and economic, GAAP profits, I’m comfortable not thinking too deeply about how this particular decision will work out for Microsoft. I will hope for, and expect, positive results.
Microsoft returns to its B2B roots, and why Apple may be helped
In its early days, Microsoft did contract software work for Apple, IBM and others. Increasingly, assuming its consumer-facing PC business (and perhaps Surface) diminishes, it can prosper returning to those B2B roots. In providing business users a Windows interface, which is a B2B function in a real sense, its larger goal will be to maximize Cloud revenues and software by subscription.
The more Microsoft goes after serving its business customers with all its energies and pours its formidable resources into new products, the more it will pressure all other competitors. The company is so well-entrenched, it should evolve more and more like an 800-pound gorilla, and a patient one. (Just remember the long period of very large losses that Microsoft endured years ago in commercializing the Xbox.)
I expect this strategy to force some defensive actions by Amazon, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), even Facebook (because of LinkedIn), possibly Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG), etc.
The only obvious big tech winner if Microsoft de-emphasizes Windows, especially for consumers, is Apple. The weighted average of probabilities would now tilt toward the Mac. If the Mac line can grow again, taking share from a PC sector wherein both the manufacturers/assemblers and Microsoft are losing interest, then Apple shareholders benefit in three ways:
Apple can sell more Macs more profitably, with less price and other competition from PCs. The long-term value of profits from the Mac increases, as visibility extends farther out now that Microsoft may be beginning a staged retreat from Windows. The Apple ecosystem strengthens as the company increasingly dominates “screens” ranging from Apple Watch-size to iPhone-size to iPad-size to PC/Mac-size.
If Apple can sell many more Macs, that would be very helpful to its valuation.
Thus, I propose there are two large-cap winners from MSFT’s apparent ongoing evolution: Microsoft itself and Apple. In other words, to some extent, a return to the ’80s.
Risks
Microsoft is in the midst of a complex transition. Competition is intense, and there are definitely no guarantees. Please consider the company’s risk disclosures in its 10-K and elsewhere before investing.
Concluding remarks – Enough good things have happened, and can happen going forward, to believe in Microsoft once again
Microsoft is hitting on almost all cylinders operationally. Growth efforts such as Azure and other Cloud-based products, and LinkedIn, are have just turned, or should soon turn, profitable and have very large profit potential in the decades ahead. The company’s existing Windows/Office/server/Xbox etc. franchises, in their various incarnations, are cash cows with long tails. Meanwhile, under new leadership, Microsoft is showing new energy and focus. This is the sort of corporate third act, or version 3.0, that Apple went through when Steve Jobs returned. With consensus EPS of about $4 for FY 2019 and $4.60 for FY 2020, and noting that Microsoft has beaten consensus handily many consensus quarters, I like the intermediate-to-long term total return upside, in large part because I like Satya Nadella, his team and the overall strategy and implementation to date.
I think the odds now favor the company delivering strong growth for years to come. If so, some modest shrinkage of its P/E could still allow low double-digit annual total returns, which is my multi-year goal in owning this name. However, as a tech stock in transition, with intense competition from many directions and with a multiple in the mid-20s, Microsoft has long-term non-trivial downside risks; even though it is a DJIA (DIA) stock, it could end up as a dog.
Thanks for reading and, if you wish, sharing your knowledge and views.
Submitted Monday evening; MSFT closed at $97.60.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL,MSFT.
